extracted.intended_audience: authors submitting short fiction (especially to Strange Horizons / similar speculative-fiction magazines)
extracted.subtask_short: submitting short fiction to Strange Horizons
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and editorial policy about preparing, submitting, and (not) withdrawing short stories submitted to Strange Horizons; covers expectations about version control, timing, and editorial workload. Aimed at helping authors avoid withdrawals and replacement-submission requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit the intended version
rubrics_metrics.description: "When you send us a story, we have to assume that that story—and that version of that story—is the story you meant to send us."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before you click submit, make absolutely certain you're sending the intended (latest) version. Open the file, review it, save the correct RTF (or required format), and confirm it's the version you want editors to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not withdraw to replace with a revised version
rubrics_metrics.description: "Just like we don't normally consider unsolicited revisions of stories we've rejected, we won't generally consider replacement versions of stories that the author has withdrawn."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you withdraw a story because you feel the version we have is worthless you may withdraw it, but you cannot then revise it and resubmit the same story to Strange Horizons. Revisions should be submitted as new, different stories elsewhere; repeated withdrawals will make editors reluctant to consider your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simultaneous submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors frequently withdraw because they sent a simultaneous submission; the editor asks: "Please don't send us simultaneous submissions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not submit the same story to multiple markets at once. If you have, and then attempt to withdraw or replace because of that, it's a problem editors discourage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do a careful—but not endless—final read before submitting
rubrics_metrics.description: "Before you submit a story to SH, read through it carefully. ... Make absolutely certain that the story is as good as you want it to be (and that you won't need to change it for at least ten weeks, since that's our max response time). Don't spend too long on this step ... but do spend a little bit of time on it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend a focused period checking for substantive problems and necessary revisions. Balance thoroughness with getting work out into the world; aim to be satisfied for the magazine's response window (~ten weeks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not re-open or re-check the story while it's under consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: "After you submit the story, don't look at it again until you hear back from us."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-reading while it's under consideration tends to surface new insecurities and minor flaws that lead to withdrawing; instead, when tempted to re-check, write something new or otherwise occupy your attention until the editors respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor typos won't cause rejection; systemic errors will
rubrics_metrics.description: "Like most editors, we would never reject a story on the basis of a couple of typos. ... If there are dozens of typos, that's more of a problem—but if there are a multitude of big mistakes, you should try to find them before submitting."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't obsess over one or two small slips; however, do proofread to avoid pervasive or large mistakes that materially harm readability and chances of acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect editor time and the editorial process
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors put submissions in a database, read them, write comments about them, discuss them, and spend time on them; requesting a version swap after they've started that work is unfair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that editors invest time and resources per submission. Asking them to discard a version they've been working on and switch to another disrupts workflows and is inconsiderate; avoid creating that situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early notices of errors are less harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: "If they tell us early enough, before we read the story, then in some sense there's no harm done—it doesn't take me that much time to do the appropriate recordkeeping. (But it does annoy me.)"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you discover you sent the wrong file, notify promptly; if the story hasn't been read yet, editors can more easily accommodate administrative fixes. Still, avoid relying on this accommodation—it's an annoyance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept editorial decisions and policies gracefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the editors be the judge of the story. "If it doesn't match our tastes, the worst that'll happen is that we'll send you a polite rejection note. (And then you can revise it to your heart's content before you send it elsewhere.) We won't mock you or blacklist you. ... Your career doesn't depend on our buying this particular story."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rejected, take it in stride; revise and submit elsewhere. Do not expect special treatment or argue repeatedly with editors about policy decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaining about the withdrawal policy is unproductive
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor notes: "it cannot have any positive consequences for you to complain to us about it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the policy is driven by volume and practicality. Complaining or protesting the rule is unlikely to help and may reflect poorly on the submitter.
